title: Seal a pipe penetration with a can of expanding spray foam
instruction: Seal the gap around the pipe where it passes through the wall with the spray foam. The can only dispenses upside down. Fill the gap only about halfway so the foam can rise.
context: Sealing the gap where a pipe, duct or cable passes through a wall, floor or top plate is routine air-sealing and pest-proofing work for construction laborers, maintenance workers, plumbers and insulation installers, and energy codes require it. Doing it with a straw-applicator foam can means holding the can inverted, steering the straw tip into a narrow ring around the pipe, working the trigger while holding the can still, and metering the foam, which doubles as it cures: too little leaves the ring open, too much mushrooms out of the wall.
setup: Station table (wood); positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left, z up from the table top. Two YAM arms, bases at y +30.5 and -30.5, start in the ready pose with the grippers open. A wall section stands across the table, its front face at x 42: a 38 mm timber rim board (spruce) with 12 mm drywall behind it, 130 wide and 130 tall, centred on y 0. A copper pipe (22.2 mm outside diameter, type L, 3/4 in nominal) runs straight through a 50 mm round hole in the rim board (and a pipe-sized hole in the drywall), centred at y 0, z 22, sticking out 9 toward the robot and 6 behind the drywall. That leaves a 14 mm ring-shaped gap all round the pipe, 38 mm deep to the drywall (60 cm3). A dark rubber mat (12 x 30 x 0.3) lies on the table against the wall, centred on y 0. A 12 oz (340 g net, about 450 g full) can of straw-applicator polyurethane gap filler, similar to GREAT STUFF Gaps & Cracks Insulating Foam Sealant (12 oz, with its straw), stands upright on the table at x 24, y 7: steel can 6.5 across and 19 tall, a 2.5-across valve cup 1 tall on top, then a small round plastic actuator 1.3 across and 2 tall. A white plastic straw (6 mm across, 19.2 long) leaves the actuator's top at 45 deg above the can's horizontal, pointing to the robot's right. Under it, a narrow plastic trigger (41.5 x 8 x 3 mm) hinged to the actuator's side 11 mm above its base, resting 10 deg below the horizontal (55 deg below the straw); pushing its end toward the can by 15 deg (about 4.5 N, 3.5 cm from the hinge) opens the valve. Nothing else is in the scene.
scoring: Scored at the wall face 30 minutes after the trial, once the foam is tack-free, from a straight-on photo with a printed transparent template laid over it: a ring of 36 sectors (10 deg each) centred on the pipe. A sector is sealed when cured foam spans the gap from the pipe to the hole's edge across the whole sector, with no opening wider than 2 mm. Coverage: 0 if fewer than 9 of the 36 sectors are sealed; 0.25 from 9; 0.5 from 18; 0.75 from 27; 1.0 from 35. Bulge, measured with a ruler laid across the face: -0.25 if foam stands more than 10 mm proud of the wall face anywhere; the score is capped at 0.5 if it stands more than 20 mm proud. Never below 0. Foam outside the gap (on the wall, the pipe, the mat or the table) is not scored: it seals nothing.
reset_notes: Polyurethane foam gives off isocyanate fumes while it cures and sticks to skin and surfaces: run trials in a ventilated area, wear nitrile gloves and safety glasses when handling the can and the board, and cover the gripper finger pads with disposable nitrile finger cots (the foam only leaves the straw tip). Each trial needs an empty gap: fit a fresh 38 mm rim-board block with a 50 mm hole (cut with a hole saw) and a clean copper stub, or cut the cured foam out flush and scrape the bore clean. Shake the can for 30 s and fit a new straw; replace the can when it no longer dispenses at full flow (a 340 g can holds about 300 cm3 of liquid, roughly 8 trials of about 38 cm3). Wipe off any uncured foam with acetone.
fidelity: Approximate. The can, straw and trigger are rigid bodies; the trigger is a hinged lever with a return spring (4.5 N at the contact point, fully pressed). The can is modelled on a 12 oz straw-applicator gap-filler can like GREAT STUFF Gaps & Cracks, not as an exact replica of it: its size, straw and trigger follow that kind of can, and the trigger force is an estimate. The foam is not simulated as a fluid: liquid leaves the straw tip at a rate set by how far the trigger is pressed (none in the first 25% of its travel, up to 6 cm3/s at full press) and only while the valve points within 60 deg of straight down (fading to none at 90 deg). Liquid that leaves the tip inside the gap is booked to its 10 deg sector; it doubles in volume as it cures, with a 3 s time constant standing in for the minutes a real can takes; excess over a sector's volume spreads to its neighbours along the gap, 2% of it per round venting out of the face as a bulge that mushrooms over three times the sector's face area. Depth is not modelled: a sector counts as sealed when its cured foam fills at least 90% of the sector's volume, standing in for the photo's check that foam spans the gap at the face (the straw puts the foam in 7 mm from the face of the 38 mm gap, so a real gap closes at the face before the back, and the stand-in is conservative). Liquid that leaves the tip anywhere else is tracked but not scored. The arms are compliant (about 7 mm per N at the fingertips), so pressing the trigger pushes the held can; the demo corrects for this with closed-loop tracking.
